extra.message: Hardcoded Weak JWT Signing Secret — Complete authentication bypass: attacker can forge JWT tokens impersonating any user (including any user_id), gaining full access to all authenticated endpoints including transfers, password changes, and PII data. [verified: JWT tokens are signed and verified with the hardcoded secret 'secret' in auth.py:20 and auth_routes.py (login endpoint). This trivially guessable string is publicly known, enabling complete authentication bypass by forging valid JWTs for any user_id with no compensating controls.]

Hardcoded Weak JWT Signing Secret — Anyone who knows the secret 'secret' (trivially guessable) can forge valid JWT tokens for any user_id, gaining full authentication as any user without credentials. [verified: The same hardcoded secret 'secret' used for JWT signing/verification (auth.py:20, auth_routes.py login endpoint) is a MISSING-CONTROL/CONFIG finding — the weak secret is genuinely present on a reachable path (login token creation and protected-endpoint verification), allowing anyone to forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs.]

SQL Injection in User Registration — Complete database compromise: read all users' password hashes, balances, PII; modify or delete records; potentially gain admin access or forge transactions. [verified: `username` from request body is interpolated via f-string at line 22: `f"INSERT INTO user ... VALUES ('{username}', ..."` and executed at line 23 with no parameterization. The ORM existence check at line 18 tests uniqueness but does not sanitize the value used in the subsequent INSERT.]

SQL Injection in User Login — Authentication bypass and database compromise: attacker can log in as any user without knowing their password, or extract all user records including password hashes and PII. [verified: `username` from request body is interpolated via f-string at line 36: `f"SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = '{username}'"` and executed at line 37 with no parameterization, enabling authentication bypass via `' OR '1'='1`.]

Insecure YAML Deserialization Leading to Remote Code Execution — Full remote code execution on the server: attacker can execute arbitrary system commands, read/write files, exfiltrate the entire database, install persistence, or pivot to internal network. [verified: `yaml.load(profile_yaml, Loader=yaml.Loader)` at line 157 deserializes user-supplied YAML with the unsafe default Loader (PyYAML 5.3.1), enabling arbitrary code execution via `!!python/object:subprocess.Popen` YAML tags.]

SQL Injection in Transaction Listing — Complete database compromise: extract any table data (users, transactions, passwords), modify or delete data, or perform denial of service via DROP statements. [verified: Finding [0]: The `user_id` query parameter flows directly into an f-string SQL query at transaction_routes.py:49 with zero parameterization, sanitization, or type coercion — attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via `?user_id=`. No middleware, decorator, or validation control exists.]

SQL Injection in Transaction Search — Complete database compromise: attacker can extract any data from any table, bypass the sender_id/receiver_id scope check, modify records, or escalate to full database control. [verified: Finding [1]: The `description` query parameter is interpolated into a raw SQL LIKE clause at transaction_routes.py:93 with no escaping or parameterization — attacker can break out of the LIKE string and execute arbitrary SQL, including bypassing the user_id scope filter. The comment on lines 91-92 even acknowledges the deliberate vulnerability.]

Debug Mode Enabled Exposing Werkzeug Debugger Console — Arbitrary code execution via Werkzeug debugger console if PIN is bypassed or known; exposure of sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII) in stack trace local variables on error pages. [verified: `debug=True` at app.py:228 enables Werkzeug's interactive debugger, which intercepts unhandled exceptions before the custom 500 handler (app.py:67-69), exposing stack traces with local variables (passwords, tokens) and providing a /console endpoint for potential RCE if the PIN is known.]

Flask Debug Mode Enabled in Production — An attacker who triggers an exception on any endpoint gains access to the Werkzeug interactive debugger, enabling arbitrary Python code execution on the server. [verified: Same root cause as finding [0]: `debug=True` at app.py:228 activates Werkzeug's debugger, exposing detailed error pages with local variables and an interactive console that can yield RCE.]

Sensitive Data (SSN, PII) Stored in Plaintext in Database — Mass PII theft: attacker who gains database access (via SQL injection, file read, or backup exposure) obtains SSN, DOB, full names, phone numbers, and addresses for all 6+ users in plaintext. [verified: models.py:15 stores profile as plaintext db.Text (json.dumps with no encryption); SSN, DOB, full name, phone, address are readable verbatim via /api/me (auth_routes.py:81-88) and exfiltratable via any of the multiple SQL injection endpoints — DB file has no encryption at rest.]

Weak Password Hashing with Unsalted MD5 — Password hash cracking: attacker who obtains the password_hash column (via SQL injection or DB access) can reverse all user passwords instantly, enabling account takeover across all users. [verified: models.py:24 uses unsalted raw MD5 via hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() in set_password/check_password — no PBKDF2/bcrypt/scrypt/argon2, no salt; hashes are reversible at billions/sec on GPU and all 6 test users share 'password123', enabling mass account takeover once the DB is obtained via SQL injection.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Brute-force password attacks: attacker can try millions of password combinations against any username without throttling, leading to account takeover. Also enables mass user enumeration and DoS via repeated registration. [verified: No rate-limiting decorator, middleware, or counter exists on `POST /api/login` (line 31), `/api/register` (line 13), or `/api/update-password` (line 139), enabling unlimited brute-force and enumeration attempts.]

Sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (SSN, DOB) Exposed in API Response — Identity theft and privacy violation: attacker with a valid (or forged) JWT can retrieve full SSN, date of birth, name, phone, and address for any user, enabling identity fraud. [verified: `current_user.get_profile()` at line 95 returns the full JSON profile including plaintext `ssn`, `dob`, `fullName`, `phone`, and `address` (seed data at app.py shows `'ssn': '123-45-6789'`), exposing sensitive PII to any authenticated session.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Update — Unlimited password change attempts enable brute-forcing user passwords or mass password resets. [verified: POST /api/update-password (line 139) has no rate limiting. With the IDOR at line 141 (user_id from request body, not JWT), any authenticated user can run unlimited password-change attempts against any target user — a direct brute-force account-takeover path.]

IDOR in Password Update — Any Authenticated User Can Change Any Other User's Password — An attacker can supply any user_id in the request body and change that user's password to a known value, achieving full account takeover. [verified: Same code path as finding [3]: `user_id` from request body (line 142) bypasses the JWT-authenticated `current_user` with no ownership check, allowing any authenticated user to change another user's password.]

Missing Input Validation on Transfer Amount (Negative/Unbounded) — Financial theft: attacker can transfer negative amounts to drain another user's balance into their own account, or transfer arbitrarily large amounts up to the full balance, bypassing business logic constraints. [verified: Finding [3]: `amount = Decimal(str(data.get('amount', 0)))` at transaction_routes.py:14 has no `amount <= 0` guard — a negative amount passes the balance check (`if balance < -1000` is False for any positive balance), then `balance -= -1000` adds to sender and `balance += -1000` subtracts from receiver, enabling theft. No upper bound exists either.]

Missing Input Validation — Negative Transfer Amount Increases Sender Balance — An attacker can arbitrarily increase their own balance by sending a negative amount, then transfer real funds out, effectively minting money. [verified: Finding [5]: Same root cause as finding [3] — `amount = Decimal(str(data.get('amount', 0)))` at transaction_routes.py:14 with no positivity validation. A negative amount inverts the intended debit/credit logic, letting the sender steal from the receiver. No intervening control (min-value check) exists.]

Race Condition / TOCTOU in Balance Transfer Allowing Double-Spending — Unlimited financial gain: attacker can submit multiple simultaneous transfer requests and spend the same balance amount multiple times, potentially draining the entire bank's funds across all user accounts. [verified: Finding [4]: The balance-check (`if current_user.balance < amount:`) at line 30 is non-atomic with the balance updates at lines 33-34, and app.py configures `isolation_level: None` (autocommit), `check_same_thread: False`, and WAL mode — concurrent requests can both pass the check before either deduction commits, enabling double-spending. No locking serializes the critical section.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in Transaction History — Horizontal privilege escalation: any authenticated user can view the full transaction history (sender, receiver, amounts, descriptions, timestamps) of any other user, violating financial privacy. [verified: Finding [2]: At transaction_routes.py:47-49, `user_id` is taken from query params with no ownership check against `current_user.id` — compare with the `get_transaction` endpoint (line 57-73) which DOES enforce ownership. No middleware/permission_classes verify the requested user_id belongs to the authenticated user.]

Permissive CORS Configuration Reflecting Arbitrary Origins with Credentials — Cross-origin data theft: any website can make credentialed requests to the API, potentially exfiltrating user data or performing actions if the victim has an active session (though JWT is localStorage-based, this CORS misconfig lowers the barrier for combined attacks). [verified: The after_request handler (app.py:49-55) reflects any Origin verbatim with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, which is a genuine CORS misconfiguration; however, since JWT is stored in localStorage (not cookies), cross-origin requests cannot automatically include the auth token, limiting the claimed account-takeover impact.]

CORS Reflects Arbitrary Origin with Credentials Enabled — Any external website can make authenticated API requests (including transfer and password-change) on behalf of logged-in users who visit that site, enabling full account takeover via CSRF-like cross-origin attacks. [verified: Same root cause as finding [1]: CORS reflects arbitrary Origin with credentials (app.py:52-55); the claim of 'full account takeover via CSRF-like attacks' is overstated because the JWT is in localStorage and not automatically sent cross-origin, but the CORS misconfiguration is still genuinely present.]

Information Exposure via 500 Error Handler — SQL injection error messages, database schema details, and internal stack traces are returned to the client, aiding further exploitation. [verified: 500 handler returns str(error) which leaks actual Python exception messages (e.g. SQL constraint names, DB error details) aiding exploitation; debug=True is a separate bigger exposure, but this handler is independently informative to an attacker.]

Missing Rate Limiting on User Registration — Unrestricted account creation allows resource exhaustion, spam accounts, and brute-force attacks on the registration endpoint. [verified: POST /api/register has no rate-limiting decorator, middleware, or IP throttle (confirmed by grep for limiter/throttle). An unauthenticated attacker can create unlimited accounts, exhausting DB storage and enabling spam — a genuine CWE-307 missing control on a reachable persistent endpoint.]

User Enumeration via Distinct Registration Error Messages — Account enumeration: attacker can build a list of valid usernames for targeted brute-force or phishing attacks, increasing the efficiency of credential stuffing attacks. [verified: Line 18 returns `{'error': 'Username already exists'}` (HTTP 400) for taken usernames versus HTTP 201 for new registrations, allowing attackers to probe which usernames exist on the system.]

No Server-Side JWT Token Invalidation on Logout — Session persistence after logout: stolen or intercepted JWT tokens remain valid for up to 24 hours even after the legitimate user logs out, allowing prolonged unauthorized access. [verified: The logout handler at line 86 returns success without any token blacklist or server-side invalidation — the comment on line 84 confirms `# JWT tokens can't be invalidated server-side` — leaving the token valid for its full 24-hour expiry.]

Unbounded YAML Input Leading to Denial of Service — Denial of service: attacker can crash the server process by sending an extremely large YAML payload that exhausts available memory during `yaml.load()`, making the application unavailable. [verified: Line 155 reads `profile_yaml` from the request body with no size limit, and `yaml.load()` at line 157 must parse the entire string into memory, allowing denial of service via multi-gigabyte payloads.]

JWT Token Stored in Browser localStorage (XSS-Exposable) — Token theft via XSS: any cross-site scripting vulnerability in the SPA allows an attacker to steal the JWT token and impersonate the victim, gaining full access to their account (transfers, PII, password changes). [verified: JWT token is stored via localStorage.setItem('token', data.token) (App.js:52) and retrieved via localStorage.getItem('token') throughout the frontend; no HttpOnly cookie or alternative script-inaccessible storage is used anywhere, leaving the token exposed to any same-origin XSS.]

Hardcoded Weak Flask SECRET_KEY — Flask session forgery: attacker can forge Flask session cookies, potentially gaining unauthorized access if any code path relies on session data for authorization decisions. [verified: SECRET_KEY='supersecret' at app.py:16 is hardcoded and weak, but Flask sessions are not used in this app (auth uses JWT with a separate 'secret' in auth.py), so forging session cookies has near-zero practical impact.]

Weak Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY — An attacker can forge Flask session cookies and exploit any Flask feature that relies on the SECRET_KEY, potentially leading to privilege escalation or RCE via session-based deserialization. [verified: Same root cause as finding [2]: SECRET_KEY 'supersecret' is hardcoded (app.py:16); the claim of 'RCE via session-based deserialization' is incorrect (Flask sessions use JSON serialization via itsdangerous, not pickle) and sessions are not used in this app.]

Missing Input Validation on User Registration — Null or empty username/password values can create malformed user accounts; very long values can cause storage exhaustion or trigger SQL errors that reveal internal details. [verified: No null/empty/length/character validation on username/password (lines 15–16). A None key inserts literal 'None'; long strings can trigger SQL errors revealing internals. However, the SQL injection via f-string is the real root cause — validation alone wouldn't fix it, so independent impact is low.]

Missing Rate Limiting on YAML Profile Import — Unlimited YAML deserialization attempts allow brute-forcing RCE payloads or causing repeated denial-of-service via resource exhaustion. [verified: POST /api/profile/import has no rate limiting, but the companion yaml.load(Loader=yaml.Loader) RCE works in one shot — rate limiting does not prevent code execution. It offers only marginal authenticated-DoS protection, so this is a defense-in-depth nit with low independent impact.]

Exception Details Leaked in YAML Import Error Response — An attacker can glean internal implementation details, library versions, and file paths from error messages, aiding further attacks. [verified: Line 165 returns `{'error': str(e)}` in the except block, leaking internal error messages (YAML parsing internals, file paths, library details) to the attacker in the HTTP response body.]

User Enumeration via Transfer Endpoint — An attacker can enumerate all valid user IDs in the system by observing the distinct 404 vs 400/200 responses, enabling targeted attacks on known accounts. [verified: Transfer endpoint (transaction_routes.py:21-24) returns 404 for non-existent to_user_id vs 400/200 for existing ones; no rate limiting, no generic error messages, and registration is open, so any authenticated attacker can enumerate valid user IDs.]

Missing Pagination on Transactions Endpoint Enables Resource Exhaustion — An attacker with a valid token can repeatedly request the full transaction history, causing excessive memory and CPU consumption on the server (denial of service). [verified: Finding [6]: The `get_transactions` query at transaction_routes.py:49 has no LIMIT/OFFSET clause, so an authenticated attacker could request all records without bound, consuming server memory. However, the transaction table contains only ~15 seeded rows, and the critical SQL injection (finding [0]) on the same endpoint already bypasses any pagination benefit — practical resource-exhaustion impact ]

Missing Pagination on Transaction Search — An attacker can trigger server resource exhaustion and denial of service by issuing search queries that match large numbers of records. [verified: Search endpoint (transaction_routes.py:88) fetches all matching rows with no LIMIT clause; though scoped to the authenticated user's own transactions, an attacker can generate many records via small transfers and issue broad searches to cause server memory exhaustion.]
